# Introduction

## Dataset description

The dataset contains the results of the 2024 European Elections for all Italian municipalities, for every party list (so, parties' voting patterns at municipality level). 
Each row represents:
- one Comune
- one party/list
- the number of votes obtained by that list in that Comune
The dataset also includes information on:
- region
- province/città metropolitana
- municipality
- electors and voters
- blank and contested ballots

The dataset was retrieved from Ministero dell'Interno as cvs.file (Eligendo website) in the folder at the following link: <https://elezionistorico.interno.gov.it/eligendo/opendata.php>

```{r}
# Defining Paths
path_data <- "~/Desktop/Data Science/R & Stats/Progetti/Roma_Italia_EU2024/Dati/LivComune_Europee_2024_IT"

# Output folders: figures and tables are written straight into the project subfolders,
# so re-rendering rebuilds the folder structure without moving files by hand.
path_out_maps    <- "~/Desktop/Data Science/R & Stats/Progetti/Roma_Italia_EU2024/Maps"
path_out_scatter <- "~/Desktop/Data Science/R & Stats/Progetti/Roma_Italia_EU2024/Scatterplots"
path_out_tables  <- "~/Desktop/Data Science/R & Stats/Progetti/Roma_Italia_EU2024/Tables"
dir.create(path_out_maps,    showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
dir.create(path_out_scatter, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
dir.create(path_out_tables,  showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

Europee24_Italia_df <- read.csv(file.path(path_data, "EUROPEE_ITALIA_LivComune.csv"))
```

```{r}
Europee24_Italia_df <- read.csv(
  file.path(path_data, "EUROPEE_ITALIA_LivComune.csv"),
  sep = ";")
```
(here I added ";" for proper visualization of the dataset)

# Turnout and abstention

## Subsetting Rome's turnout data by province

So: only Rome considered as province (all constituencies within Rome province)
```{r}
rome_province <- Europee24_Italia_df[Europee24_Italia_df$DESCPROVINCIA == "ROMA",]

head(rome_province, n=10)
```
## Subsetting Rome's turnout data by municipality(commune)

So: only Rome considered as municipality ("comune di Roma") (all constitiuencies within Rome province)
```{r}
rome_comune <- Europee24_Italia_df[Europee24_Italia_df$DESCCOMUNE == "ROMA",]

head(rome_comune, n=10)
```

## Electors vs Voters

**Electors** are individuals who are eligible to vote (they have the right to vote but not necessarily have cast a vote at the 2024 European Elections.

**Voters** are those who actually cast a vote at these elections.

By definition:
Voters ≤ Electors and from their gap we can obtain the **abstention level**.
```{r}
mean(Europee24_Italia_df$ELETTORI, na.rm = TRUE)
```
Average of electors in Italy at the 2024 European Elections. 

na.rm = TRUE is used to remove missing values (NA)

```{r}
mean(Europee24_Italia_df$VOTANTI, na.rm=TRUE)
```
Average of voters in Italy at the 2024 European Elections. 

## Levels of Turnout and abstention

The dataset is at municipality (Comune) level for the whole of Italy.
Average number of electors per municipality (Italy):
6,264.789
Average number of voters per municipality (Italy):
3,118.848
This means that, on average, **only about half** of the eligible electors actually voted.

The *gap* between electors and voters reflects *voter abstention*.

So, at the national level:
the average Italian municipality shows significant non-participation
and turnout is well below full electoral participation
This difference provides a first descriptive indication of electoral abstention patterns across Italian municipalities at the more recent elections comprising the whole national territory (this is why I chose the dataframe from these elections)

## Rome Province/Città Metropolitana

We can do the same reasoning if we subset at the province level (more accurately, Città Metropolitana) focusing on Rome province/città metropolitana:
```{r}
mean(rome_province$ELETTORI, na.rm =TRUE)
mean(rome_province$VOTANTI, na.rm =TRUE)
```
Average electors (Rome province):
28,571.64
Average voters (Rome province):
12,876.02
This indicates that, even in the **Rome province**, **less than half** of eligible electors actually voted on average
The gap between electors and voters *again reflects electoral abstention*, this time within a more urbanized and populous context compared to the national average.

## Rome Municipality
```{r}
mean(rome_comune$ELETTORI, na.rm=TRUE)
mean(rome_comune$VOTANTI, na.rm =TRUE)
```

Also in this case, the electors–voters gap remains remarkably stable across different territorial levels:
National (average Italian municipality)
Province of Rome (average municipality within the province/città metropolitana)
Municipality of Rome (Rome city itself) - in this case the mean corresponds to the actual numbers of both electors and voters because the dataframe is at municipality level and Rome as municipality appears multiple times. This is shaped by how European elections are territorially organized and the design of the electoral constituencies (I think) (to see in detail maybe).

### Interpretation

In all cases, voters are **the half** of the electors, suggesting a **structural pattern of electoral participation** with **significant abstention across all the territorial units** of the dataframe of the 2024 EU elections in Italy.

## Gender gap

We can also check the gender gap across the territorial units of interest.

Average of male and female voters (Rome province)
```{r}
mean(rome_province$VOTANTI_M, na.rm =TRUE)
mean(rome_province$VOTANTI_F, na.rm =TRUE)
```

Average of male and female voters (Rome municipality)
```{r}
mean(rome_comune$VOTANTI_M, na.rm =TRUE)
mean(rome_comune$VOTANTI_F, na.rm =TRUE)
```

## Turnout rates across three levels

*Turnout rate* = voters / electors (proportion)
This measures participation, not population size.

### Turnout Italy

Here we compute turnout using average values across all Italian municipalities (so, the average is **national** but at the municipality level, so the mean refers to the ration between electors and voters in all Italian municipalities of the dataframe)

```{r}
library(dplyr)

turnout_italy <- Europee24_Italia_df %>%
  summarise(turnout = mean(VOTANTI / ELETTORI, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
mutate(turnout_pct = turnout * 100)

turnout_italy
```
So: the national turnout of all Italian cities/municipalities at the 2024 EU elections was roughly 52%, so the ***average municipal turnout***. 

### Turnout of all provinces within the dataframe
```{r}
turnout_by_province <- Europee24_Italia_df %>%
  filter(!is.na(DESCPROVINCIA),
         DESCPROVINCIA != "") %>%
  group_by(DESCPROVINCIA) %>%
  summarise(
    turnout_pct = 100 * sum(VOTANTI, na.rm = TRUE) /
                          sum(ELETTORI, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

head(turnout_by_province, n=10)
```
This is the table with the % turnout levels of all **Italian Provinces** at the 2024 EU elections.

### Min and Max Turnout at Province Level

This is the province with the lowest turnout: NUORO.
```{r}
min_turnout_prov_it <- min(turnout_by_province$turnout_pct, na.rm = TRUE)

lowest_turnout_prov_it <- turnout_by_province %>%
  filter(turnout_pct == min_turnout_prov_it)

lowest_turnout_prov_it
```
And the province with the highest turnout: FIRENZE
```{r}
max_turnout_prov_it <- max(turnout_by_province$turnout_pct, na.rm = TRUE)

highest_turnout_prov_it <- turnout_by_province %>%
  filter(turnout_pct == max_turnout_prov_it)

highest_turnout_prov_it
```
## Turnout all municipalities within the dataframe

```{r}
turnout_by_comune <- Europee24_Italia_df %>%
  filter(!is.na(DESCPROVINCIA),
         DESCPROVINCIA != "") %>%
  group_by(DESCCOMUNE) %>%
  summarise(
    turnout_pct = 100 * sum(VOTANTI, na.rm = TRUE) /
                          sum(ELETTORI, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )   

turnout_by_comune
```
Also here we may find out with the highest and the lowest turnout levels of Italian municipalities.

## Turnout of Rome as province and as municipality

First, we need to extract/subset Rome as province and as municipalities from turnout_by_province and turnout_by_municipality.

```{r}
turnout_rome_province <- turnout_by_province %>%
  filter(DESCPROVINCIA == "ROMA")

turnout_rome_province
```
This is the turnout of Rome as province/città metropolitana from the dataset of all Italian provinces.

```{r}
turnout_rome_comune <- turnout_by_comune %>%
  filter(DESCCOMUNE == "ROMA")

turnout_rome_comune
```


This is the turnout of Rome as municipality from the dataset of all Italian municipalities.

## Levels of Turnout across Territorial Units

This is how to display the three levels of turnout across the territorial units of analysis.
```{r}
bind_rows(
  Italy = turnout_italy,
  Roma_Città_Metropolitana = turnout_rome_province,
  Roma_Comune = turnout_rome_comune,
  .id = "territorial unit")
```
What emerges here is, as said previously, a **systematic "non-voting" pattern** reflecting high abstention across the territorial units under analysis. 
Drawing on ***"geography of discontent"*** literature (Rodrìguez-Pose, Crulli, Pinto,...) cities and in general urban areas display higher levels of political participation compared to rural areas. 

However, the city of Rome is not above the national average, and if we take Rome as municipality turnout is even lower (at least at the 2024 EU elections).
The finding also conflicts with the general assumption that capital cities are more politically active.

Can it be the first finding of the analysis? If decide to explore more in detail, I may want to compare Rome with more rural towns and areas to study the relationship between political participation and urban/rural areas.

## Mapping Turnout at Provincial Level

```{r}
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(stringr)
library(ggplot2)

# Reading Shapefile provinces (from ISTAT)
prov_shape_clean <- st_read("~/Desktop/Data Science/R & Stats/Dati_geografici/Limiti01012024/ProvCM01012024") %>%
  mutate(
    # se DEN_PROV è "-", usa DEN_CM (es. Torino, Roma...)
    join_name = if_else(DEN_PROV == "-", DEN_CM, DEN_PROV),
    # normalizza (maiuscolo + spazi sistemati)
    join_name = str_squish(str_to_upper(join_name))
  )

# Cleaning turnout by province
turnout_by_province_clean <- turnout_by_province %>%
  mutate(
    join_name = str_squish(str_to_upper(DESCPROVINCIA)),
    # fixing mismatch
    join_name = case_when(
      join_name == "REGGIO NELL' EMILIA" ~ "REGGIO NELL'EMILIA",
      join_name == "MASSA-CARRARA"       ~ "MASSA CARRARA",
      join_name == "REGGIO EMILIA"       ~ "REGGIO NELL'EMILIA",
      join_name == "REGGIO CALABRIA"     ~ "REGGIO DI CALABRIA",
      TRUE ~ join_name
    )
  ) %>%
  select(join_name, turnout_pct)

# Left Join shape files and fdi dataframe
turnout_by_province_map <- left_join(prov_shape_clean, turnout_by_province_clean, by = "join_name")

# check (should be 0 otherwise grey areas in the map)
sum(is.na(turnout_by_province_map$turnout_pct))

# Plot
turnout_by_province_plot <- ggplot(turnout_by_province_map) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = turnout_pct), color = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "OrRd", direction = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Turnout share by province (EU elections 2024)",
    fill  = "Turnout share (%)"
  ) +
  theme_bw()

# Save plot
ggsave(file.path(path_out_maps, "turnout_share_province_EU2024.pdf"),
       plot = turnout_by_province_plot,
       width = 8,
       height = 10)

# Print the map in R:
turnout_by_province_plot
```
# FDI voting patterns

What is the relationship between turnout and Fratelli d'Italia (FDI) voting pattern?

I choose this party because:
– it is the main governing party in Italy;
– the EU elections took place two years after FDI’s national electoral victory, making them a useful opportunity to assess levels of post-government electoral consensus;
– according to mainstream academic literature, FDI is widely regarded as a populist party and represents one of the most significant contemporary cases of populism in Europe, in line with established definitions proposed by scholars such as Cas Mudde and Simon Tormey.

Subsetting FDI from the dataframe (and printing only the first three entries):
```{r}
fdi <- Europee24_Italia_df %>%
  filter(DESCLISTA == "FRATELLI D'ITALIA", VOTANTI > 0)

head(fdi, n=3)
```

```{r}
fdi_mun_italy <- fdi %>%
  summarise(
    vote_share = sum(NUMVOTI, na.rm = TRUE) / sum(Europee24_Italia_df$NUMVOTI, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    vote_share_pct = vote_share * 100)

fdi_mun_italy
```
This is the **FDI voting share average of a typical Italian municipality** (so, national average but at municipality level, because the dataset of interest is ***municipality-centered***)

## FDI by province

FDI voting share across all Italian provinces of the dataset (I print only the first three entries for convenience):

sum(NUMVOTI) / sum(VOTANTI) = real weight of province/comune or any territorial unit

```{r}
library(dplyr)
# Totale voti validi per comune (tutte le liste) per valid votes per denominatore vote share
total_valid_votes_by_province <- Europee24_Italia_df %>%
  group_by(DESCPROVINCIA) %>%
  summarise(
    total_valid_votes = sum(NUMVOTI, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

fdi_by_province <- fdi %>%
  group_by(DESCPROVINCIA) %>%
  summarise(
    fdi_votes = sum(NUMVOTI, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  left_join(total_valid_votes_by_province, by = "DESCPROVINCIA") %>%
  mutate(
    vote_share_pct = 100 * fdi_votes / total_valid_votes
  )

head(fdi_by_province, n = 10)
```

## FDI by comune (at municipal level)

FDI voting share across all Italian muncipalities of the dataset (I print only the first three entries for convenience):
```{r}
# Totale voti validi per comune (tutte le liste) per valid votes per denominatore vote share
total_valid_votes_by_comune <- Europee24_Italia_df %>%
  group_by(DESCCOMUNE) %>%
  summarise(
    total_valid_votes = sum(NUMVOTI, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Voti FDI per comune
fdi_by_comune <- fdi %>%
  group_by(DESCCOMUNE) %>%
  summarise(
    fdi_votes = sum(NUMVOTI, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  left_join(total_valid_votes_by_comune, by = "DESCCOMUNE") %>%
  mutate(
    vote_share_pct = 100 * fdi_votes / total_valid_votes
  )

head(fdi_by_comune, n = 10)
```

## FDI in Rome

FDI vote share in the province/città metropolitana of Rome:
```{r}
fdi_rome_province <- fdi_by_province %>%
  filter(DESCPROVINCIA == "ROMA")

fdi_rome_province
```
FDI vote share in the municipality of Rome:

```{r}
fdi_rome_comune <- fdi_by_comune %>%
  filter(DESCCOMUNE == "ROMA")

fdi_rome_comune
```
It is interesting to note how FDI voting share within **the province of Rome** is **above** of Rome as municipality and the average of all Italian municipalities.

# PRPP in Italy

PRRP vote share = FdI + Lega vote share combined.

Below the combined vote shares at various unit of analysis.

First, the PRRP vote share at national level weigheted at municipality level.

```{r}
prrp_mun_italy <- fdi_mun_italy %>%
  mutate(prrp_vote_share_pct = vote_share_pct + lega_mun_italy$vote_share_pct) %>%
  select(prrp_vote_share_pct)

prrp_mun_italy
```
## PRRP by Province

PRRP = FdI + Lega , so: Combined Lega–FDI vote share by PROVINCE / CITTA METROPOLITANA (ofc rightly weighted)

```{r}
prrp_by_province <- left_join(
  fdi_by_province,
  lega_by_province,
  by = "DESCPROVINCIA",
  suffix = c("_fdi", "_lega")
) %>%
  mutate(
    prrp_vote_share_pct = vote_share_pct_fdi + vote_share_pct_lega
  ) %>%
  select(DESCPROVINCIA, prrp_vote_share_pct)

head(prrp_by_province, n = 10)
```

# Bivariate Analysis: Correlations between Turnout & Vote Share at Provincial Level 

## Turnout and FDI

Now we can directly observe and compare the turnout and FDI vote share at the territorial unit we are interested in.

For now, let's choose at province level by performing a left join of the two datasets of turnout and FDI vote share previously created:
```{r}
province_merged_fdi <- left_join(turnout_by_province, fdi_by_province, by = c("DESCPROVINCIA"="DESCPROVINCIA")) %>%
  transmute(
    DESCPROVINCIA,
    turnout_pct = turnout_pct,
    fdi_vote_share_pct = vote_share_pct)

head(province_merged_fdi, n=10)
```
To make it more readable and straightforward, I inserted only the % of both turnout and FDI vote share.

### Scatterplot of Turnout-FDI vote share (Province-level)

```{r}
library(ggplot2)

province_merged_fdi_fig1 <- ggplot(province_merged_fdi, mapping = aes(x=turnout_pct, y=fdi_vote_share_pct)) +
  geom_point()+
  xlab("Turnout Provinces") + ylab("FDI Vote Share in Provinces")+
  ggtitle("Turnout and Voting Pattern")+
  theme_bw()+
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se=FALSE)+
  scale_x_continuous(breaks=seq(30, 70, by = 10), limits = c(30,70))+
  scale_y_continuous(breaks=seq(10, 50, by = 10), limits = c(10,50))

province_merged_fdi_fig1
```
This scatterplot reveals a **weak-to-moderate positive association** between turnout and FDI vote share at the provincial level, as the fitting line is slightly upward but datapoints widely scattered.

At the same time, the wide dispersion of observations around the regression line suggests that turnout alone explains only a limited portion of the variation in FDI vote share across provinces.

So, turnout alone *cannot* be considered as an important variable to explain the variation in FDI voting pattern across Italian provinces, and both variables are weakly associated.

(to see in detail as I am not entirely familiar with the precise terminology)

### Correlation

Since the scatter plot suggests a slightly positive, moderate but noisy association (with widely dispersed data points) between turnout and FDI vote share at the provincial level, we quantify this relationship using Pearson’s correlation coefficient (r)

```{r}
cor(
  province_merged_fdi$turnout_pct,
  province_merged_fdi$fdi_vote_share_pct,
  method = "pearson",
  use = "complete.obs")
```
An r of 0.50 indicates a ***moderate positive linear association*** (between r=1 as perfect positive correlation and r=0 as no linear correlation): provinces with higher turnout tend to display higher FDI vote shares, although the correlation is not sufficiently clear because not perfect linear (r is low) and noisy (many datapoints dispersed and widely scattered).

### Statistical significance

```{r}
cor.test(
  province_merged_fdi$turnout_pct,
  province_merged_fdi$fdi_vote_share_pct,
  method = "pearson")
```
From this test we can identify:
- r is 0.4954528 (as explained earlier);
- p-value is 1.907 × 10⁻⁹ (p < 0.001), which implies that the correlation is highly statistically significant;

Therefore, although the **correlation is moderate in strength, it is statistically robust**, suggesting that higher turnout is moderately but systematically (and statistically significant) associated with higher FDI vote share across Italian provinces.

### Definitive scatterplot

Let's graph a more detailed scatterplot with the new findings and I will try to insert Rome and Milan (as the major and the most politically significant provinces in Italy) to compare them with the other provinces of the scatterplot.

```{r}
rome_milan_province_merged_fdi <- province_merged_fdi %>%
  dplyr::filter(DESCPROVINCIA %in% c("ROMA", "MILANO"))

rome_milan_province_merged_fdi
```
This is to show the differences in terms of turnout and FDI vote share between Rome and Milan:
- in terms of turnout, Milan is slightly higher than Rome (as province);
- in terms of FDI vote share, Rome is moderately and significantly higher than Milan (always as province).

```{r}
library(ggpubr)
library(ggrepel)

province_merged_fdi_fig2 <- ggplot(
  province_merged_fdi,
  aes(x = turnout_pct, y = fdi_vote_share_pct)
) +
geom_point(size = 2.5, alpha = 0.7) +
geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "steelblue", linewidth = 1) +
  
stat_cor(
  method = "pearson",
  aes(label = paste(..r.label.., ..p.label.., sep = "~`,`~")),
  label.x.npc = "left",
  label.y.npc = "top",
  size = 4
  ) +
  
  geom_label_repel(
    data = rome_milan_province_merged_fdi,
    aes(
      x = turnout_pct,
      y = fdi_vote_share_pct,
      label = DESCPROVINCIA
    ),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    size = 4,
    box.padding = 0.5,
    point.padding = 0.3,
    segment.size = 0.6,
    force = 2,
    seed = 123
  ) +
  
  labs(
    x = "Turnout (Provinces)",
    y = "FDI Vote Share (Provinces)",
    title = "Turnout and FDI Vote Share at the Provincial Level"
  ) +
  
  theme_bw() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(30, 70, 10)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(10, 50, 10)) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(30, 70), ylim = c(10, 50))

province_merged_fdi_fig2
```
So, this new scatterplot is more precise as it shows the r Pearson correlation and the p value (above) as they indicate the direction and the statistical significant of the correlation.

It also indicates the precise location of the provinces of Rome and Milan within all the provinces of the dataset.
- Rome lies above the regression line, so FDI’s vote share in Rome exceeds what would be predicted by turnout alone.
- Milan, by contrast, lies close to the fitted regression line, suggesting that its FDI vote share is well predicted by turnout and closely reflects the average pattern of all Italian provinces.

Overall, the substantial dispersion of data points around the regression line indicates marked heterogeneity across provinces. This “noisy” pattern (widely dispersed observations) coexists with a statistically significant and moderately positive association between turnout and FDI vote share at provincial level, from the 2024 European elections.

### R²

As we said, the substantial dispersion of observations around the regression line indicates that turnout alone accounts for ***only part*** of the observed variation. But ***how much?*** 
```{r}
model <- lm(fdi_vote_share_pct ~ turnout_pct, data = province_merged_fdi)
summary(model)$r.squared
```
The estimated **R²** suggests that **approximately 25% of the cross-provincial variation in FDI vote share** is associated with turnout differences, leaving most of the vote share variation to be explained by other political, social, and contextual factors that i will examine in the multivariate analysis.

```{r}

```

Turnout is positively but weakly correlated with Lega vote share at the provincial level and statistically significant (r ≈ 0.20 ; p ≈ 0.037). The model explains only about 4% of the variation in Lega electoral support, suggesting that turnout plays a limited role in explaining Lega’s territorial performance.

Turnout is positively correlated with the vote share of both Fratelli d’Italia and the Lega at the provincial level, but the strength of the relationship differs substantially. 

For Fratelli d’Italia, the correlation is moderate (r ≈ 0.50) and highly statistically significant (p < 0.001), with turnout explaining about 25% of the variation in provincial vote share (R² ≈ 0.25). 

In contrast, the relationship between turnout and the Lega’s vote share is much weaker (r ≈ 0.20) and less significant at the 5% level (p ≈ 0.037), with turnout accounting for only about 4% of the variation (R² ≈ 0.04). 

Overall, turnout appears to be substantially more associated with the territorial variation of Fratelli d’Italia’s electoral performance than with that of the Lega.

```{r}
      label = DESCPROVINCIA
    ),

province_merged_prrp_fig1
```

```{r}
cor.test(
  province_merged_prrp$turnout_pct,
  province_merged_prrp$prrp_vote_share_pct
)
```
```{r}
model_prrp <- lm(prrp_vote_share_pct ~ turnout_pct, data = province_merged_prrp)
summary(model_prrp)$r.squared
```

When combining the vote shares of Fratelli d’Italia and the Lega to construct the PRRP vote share, the relationship with turnout becomes stronger than for the Lega alone. The correlation between turnout and the combined PRRP vote share is positive and moderate (r ≈ 0.45) and highly statistically significant (p ≈ 1.34 × 10⁻⁶). The regression model explains about 20% of the variation in PRRP vote share across provinces (R² ≈ 0.20). This suggests that turnout is meaningfully associated with the territorial variation of the populist radical right vote, although the relationship is largely driven by Fratelli d’Italia rather than by the Lega.

This pattern is consistent with the recent transformation of the Italian radical right, where Fratelli d’Italia has expanded its electoral support across territories, while the Lega remains more territorially anchored and less strongly associated with turnout variation.

# Multivariate Analysis: Correlations between Turnout & Vote Share at Provincial Level after controlling for other variables

Let's load the table with the relevant control variables:
- density population share as proxy for urbanization
- foreign population share
- GDP per capita adjusted for ppp
All variables are at provincial/città metropolitana level.

```{r}
library(readxl)

path_data <- "~/Desktop/Data Science/Excel & Stats"

data_reg24 <- read_excel("~/Desktop/Data Science/Excel & Stats/Complete_dataset.xlsx",
  sheet = "data for regression")
```

```{r}
glimpse(data_reg24)
names(data_reg24)
```
After checking teh names of the columns, I rename my variables (all from the same file) for the multivariate regression:
```{r}
data_reg24_clean <- data_reg24 %>%
  rename(
    prrp = `PRRP vote share`,
    turnout = Turnout,
    density = Density,
    foreign_population = `Foreign pop.`,
    gdp_ppp = `GDP per capita (PPP)`
  )
```

## Multivariate regression

Now I can compute the multivariate regression with all the variables from the same files: dependent, independent, control variables.

```{r}
model_prrp24 <- lm(
  prrp ~ turnout + density + foreign_population + gdp_ppp,
  data = data_reg24_clean)

summary(model_prrp24) #this stamps the full output of the multiv regression
```

Definitive table:

```{r}
library(modelsummary)

modelsummary(
  model_prrp24,
  stars = TRUE,
  title = "OLS model of PRRP vote share across Italian provinces from 2024 EU Elections")
```

Here the table is saved as png file.

```{r}
# install.packages("modelsummary")
# install.packages("webshot2")

library(modelsummary)

modelsummary(
  model_prrp24,
  stars = TRUE,
  title = "OLS model of PRRP vote share across Italian provinces from 2024 EU Elections",
output = file.path(path_out_tables, "multiv_regression_table24.png"))
```


```{r}
mun_shape_clean <- mun_shape %>%
  mutate(
    join_name = str_squish(str_to_upper(COMUNE))
  )
```
Standardizzare i nomi nello shapefiles dei comuni
	•	**str_to_upper()** → mette tutto in maiuscolo
	•	**str_squish()** → toglie spazi doppi o strani
	Serve a costruire una versione “standardizzata” dei nomi dei comuni nello shapefile.

Esempio:
	•	Agliè → AGLIÈ
	•	Roma → ROMA
```{r}
turnout_by_comune_clean <- turnout_by_comune %>%
  mutate(
    join_name = str_squish(str_to_upper(DESCCOMUNE))
  ) %>%
  select(join_name, turnout_pct)
```
Qui, stessa per i dati elettorali dei comuni

```{r}
setdiff(turnout_by_comune_clean$join_name, mun_shape_clean$join_name)
setdiff(mun_shape_clean$join_name, turnout_by_comune_clean$join_name)
```
Qui confronto i due insiemi con **setdiff**:
questi sono i nomi che stanno nel dataset elettorale ma non nello shapefile per diversità accenti/apostrofi.

Questo per sistemare i mismatch

```{r}
setdiff(turnout_by_comune_newclean$join_name, mun_shape_clean$join_name)
setdiff(mun_shape_clean$join_name, turnout_by_comune_newclean$join_name)
```
Confronto di nuovo, ne rimangono ancora alcuni.
These mismtches are due to newer *administrative merges* reflected in the electoral dataset but noy by the shapefile.

```{r}
mun_shape_newclean <- mun_shape_clean %>%
  mutate(
    join_name = case_when(
      join_name == "ALANO DI PIAVE" ~ "SETTEVILLE",
      join_name == "QUERO VAS" ~ "SETTEVILLE",
      join_name == "VIGHIZZOLO D'ESTE" ~ "SANTA CATERINA D'ESTE",
      join_name == "CARCERI" ~ "SANTA CATERINA D'ESTE",
      join_name == "GAMBUGLIANO" ~ "SOVIZZO",
      TRUE ~ join_name
    )
  )
```

```{r}
setdiff(turnout_by_comune_newclean$join_name, mun_shape_newclean$join_name)
setdiff(mun_shape_newclean$join_name, turnout_by_comune_newclean$join_name)
```
We can finally perform the leftjoin for the map
```{r}
# Left Join shapefile comuni + turnout
turnout_by_comune_map <- left_join(
  mun_shape_newclean,
  turnout_by_comune_newclean,
  by = "join_name")
# check with this: should be 0 in output otherwise grey areas for N/A
sum(is.na(turnout_by_comune_map$turnout_pct))
```

Plot & Save Plot

```{r}
  labs(
    title = "Turnout share by municipality (EU elections 2024)",
    fill  = "Turnout share (%)"
```

```{r}
# Plot

    title = "PRRPs share by municipality (EU elections 2024)",

  ) +
```

```{r}
prrp_roma_map <- prrp_by_comune_map %>%

    title = "PRRPs share in the municipalities of the Metropolitan City of Rome (EU elections 2024)",

  ) +

)
```
